content_excerpt: The Nvidia GPU was originally built to shade pixels, and every Nvidia generation since 2017 has bolted on another piece of AI-specific hardware to fix the bottleneck the previous one exposed. Volta added Tensor Cores, Hopper added TMA for tile data movement between HBM and SRAM, and Blackwell added Tensor Memory for accumulating. Nvidia removed many hardware units that are required to render graphics for their datacenter GPUs In comparison, the Trainium microarchitecture is built ground-up specifically for ML workloads, with tiles as a first-class primitive instead of having a sea of threads and then bolting on tensor/tile compute and data movement engines. Trainium3 behaves the way the physics says it should. In this past this meant software was a humongous challenge, but now no longer. 7 months later, Trainium 3 and TPUs are live on InferenceX , both trading blows or even winning vs Nvidia GB300 in cost to generate tokens at TCO. We will dive into those details below. This advantage is not purely due to Amazon’s ultra low cost supply chain. It's also due to microarchitectural decisions, which we will dive into in this post. For example, using the Trainium Descriptor Generation Engines (DGE), the equivalent of Nvidia TMA and AMD MI455X TDM, our microbenchmarks show that Trainium can reach peak HBM bandwidth utilization (MBU) at small message sizes, which is not possible on Nvidia GPUs. Furthermore, our testing covers cycle-level SRAM scratchpad latency and bandwidth testing (SBUF to PSUM), rack-scale bandwidth and latency microbenchmarks, attention exponential testing, and the precise cycle-level latency of different shapes, including how different attention head_dim (K) would affect the percentage of roofline. Every result comes from UBenchX, our microbenchmark suite, and we model each unit from first principles before we measure it. We thank Nafea Bshara (Co-Founder of AWS Annapurna Labs), Ron Diamant (Trainium Chief Architect), Michael Shteinbok, Armin Ebrahim and the rest of their team for helping teach us their architecture and validate our benchmark experiments. Star the InferenceX & UBenchX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful ! InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, OpenAI Jalapeño, Nvidia Rubin NVL72, AMD, and now, Trainium3. title: Verifiable Social Reasoning for LLM Assistants
story_key: story|title:verifiable social reasoning for llm assistants
content_excerpt: Zorik Gekhman, Senior Research Scientist; Amir Taubenfeld, Staff Research Engineer; Google Research We introduce an evaluation framework based on multi-agent social simulations that quantifies how well AI assistants understand social situations from users' subjective narratives. In our framework, a target agent with a hidden motive interacts with other agents including one representing the user, who then consults the evaluated assistant to infer the target’s motive, providing verifiable ground truth by construction. Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for everyday personal support and advice, yet evaluating their social reasoning in such consultation settings remains challenging since (1) it requires setups where the assistant learns about social situations from subjective user narratives, and (2) social properties, such as others’ intentions, typically lack verifiable ground truth. Designed to address both of these challenges, we introduce an evaluation framework for social reasoning based on multi-agent simulations. In our framework, a target agent is assigned a hidden motive and interacts with other agents, including one representing the user. The user then consults with the evaluated assistant, which must infer the target's hidden motive. Evaluating a diverse range of LLMs through our framework reveals that relying on subjective user mediation substantially complicates social reasoning. Furthermore, models are sensitive to user framing, require more detail than humans need to reach correct predictions, and fail to fully leverage clarification questions. We open-source the framework and dataset to encourage future research on user-mediated social reasoning. AI assistants operate within a user-mediated reality: the assistant hears about social events only through the subjective lens of the user, making it challenging to reason objectively about the true motive of an actor in the user’s circle. When evaluating LLMs’ social reasoning, it’s important to recognize that deployed assistants operate within a user-mediated reality . In classical reasoning tasks like math and code, LLMs operate over objective, complete information. However, when an LLM acts as a conversational assistant and is asked for personal support and advice, it does not observe the actual social interactions firsthand; its only source of information is the subjective, potentially biased lens of the user. title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.

title: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon
story_key: model:llama|title:introducing the llama cpp benchmark dashboard for amd ryzen and radeon
content_excerpt: The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance. You can choose Hardware , Model , and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201). Both tests start at context depth zero ( n_depth=0 ). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput ( avg_ts ). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows. We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh , the build and installation project behind llama.app . The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration. The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M , Q8_0 , other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16 . The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model. Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl . Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename. Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run. Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard , inspect the data , and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL
summary: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.

title: Why I'm Bullish on MCP for 2027
summary: Early MCP deserved its backlash. Code Mode, typed outputSchema, native multimodality, Agent Skills inside MCP, always-on MCP Events, and MCP Apps are turning it into the integration layer for agent harnesses in 2027.
story_key: story|title:why i m bullish on mcp for 2027
content_excerpt: MCP went through the full hype cycle in the last 18 months. Early excitement turned into backlash and confusion fast, with context bloat as the main complaint. When Skills arrived, most developers moved to CLIs and progressive disclosure instead. I never believed in that, and that sentiment is now changing. At Linear and Notion , agents now create roughly half of all issues (~2.4M/week) and pages, with Notion reporting 60x MCP traffic growth. At Atlassian , MCP handles over 5M tool calls per workday, and 44% of those users sit outside software teams where CLIs were never an option. At Neon , agent usage over MCP grows 14% week over week, and even Apple now ships local MCP servers for Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. The protocol is healthy and actively improving. The 2026-07-28 spec dropped stateful sessions and added official extensions, and clients are getting smarter about how they use them. Real tasks almost always take more than 1 tool call, e.g. you list open issues, grab details, check errors, and write a summary. With plain tool calling, every step needs another model turn and dumps information into the context. Joining data across 2 MCP servers uses the model's context as memory for intermediate payloads. Code Mode is changing how agents call MCP servers. Instead of putting 50 tool schemas into the prompt and calling 1 tool per turn, the harness gives the model a sandbox and exposes MCP tools as callable functions. It's already becoming the default in OpenCode 2.0, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Pi, and Factory Droid. Code Mode works best when the model knows what a tool returns before writing code. When an MCP server declares outputSchema alongside inputSchema , the client can generate typed stubs upfront and pass back structuredContent directly. The model chains multiple calls in 1 script, filters and joins in memory where compute is cheap, and returns only what matters. Compared to CLIs, MCP servers are natively multimodal. A tool call can return typed structuredContent for code alongside separate image, audio, or embedded resource blocks. Auth is also cleaner. CLIs and raw curl force you to store API keys on disk or in environment variables with broad permissions. An MCP client handles per-user OAuth 2.1 login flows and scoped tool permissions outside the sandbox, so connecting a remote SaaS product works without handing raw credentials to the agent. title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.

content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
story_key: story|title:swarms flocks gangs how to build train and evaluate multi agent systems
content_excerpt: This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.

title: Introducing Search for Agents

story_key: story|title:introducing search for agents
content_excerpt: AI Search , our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages. Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it. Today we're introducing Search for Agents , which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain. The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents , where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level. You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions : Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits ). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works. You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view: The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options. Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall ( WAF ) configurations). title: vllm v0.34.0
summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 In most cases it's now best to not set gpu_memory_utilization. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR
Mistral Large 4 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. #64534
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.

  • Removed:
    • QuTLASS and the fp_quant method (#65230).
    • Marlin INT8/FP8-activation (W4A8) paths and VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE; use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG (#65542).

  • Model and plugin code: all process_weights_after_loading hooks share one signature and the loader runs every module's hook (#57678); config compute_hash() replaced by compile_factors() / hash_config() (#65652).
  • API behavior:
    • llama3_json no longer streams tool arguments incrementally (#63569).
    • Canary transcription without language returns 400 (#65445).
    • An empty tools array is accepted in both frontends (#65547, #65854).
    • /v1/systemone rejects request-supplied chat templates without --trust-request-chat-template (#64503).
    • LoRA adapters on modules vLLM does not wrap are refused (#63489); misconfigured NCCL weight transfer raises (#57022).

  • New defaults:
    • Extensible KV cache (#56492); block size 64 (#63231); best-effort NUMA binding (#61258).
    • Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill at 1024 or more prefill tokens (#63956); MLA decode up-projection before the A2A merge (#64994).
    • VLLM_COMPILE_ON_ONE_RANK (#63247); minimum valid EPLB num_redundant_experts (#30614).
    • HiSparse on the extensible KV cache (#65214); encoder CUDA graphs up to encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget=5120, eager above (#65227).
